1:
The witnesses open on the psalm’s inscription before they reach its first cry, and they linger over the two technical words that head it. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry explains that David, having penned the psalm by divine inspiration for the use of the church, delivered it to the chief Musician, the master of the song who presided over the temple singers set in their classes in 1 Chron. 25; it was to be sung on Neginoth, the stringed instruments played with the hand and named again in Hab. 3:19, though now, he adds, the melody is chiefly to be made in the heart. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke derives Neginoth from a root meaning to strike, takes it of stringed instruments in general while owning that the precise sense of these musical terms is known to no man, and reads the whole as an evening hymn sung by David and his company before rest. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch set it beside the morning hymn that precedes it, calling this the Davidic evening hymn, its kinship with the third psalm betrayed by their shared formula “many say,” and note that the heading “to the chief Musician” meets us here for the first of its many appearances across the Psalter.

Then the prayer itself, “Hear me when I call, O God of my righteousness.” The reformed John Gill reads the address as a plea to a righteous God who is also the vindicator of David’s innocence and the author of his righteousness, the God who justifies him through the imputed righteousness of his Son. John Calvin, another reformed voice, hears the same title as “the maintainer of my right”: condemned by men and borne down by slander, David appeals from the perverse judgment of the crowd to the One who alone defends his cause, and Calvin refers the psalm not to Absalom’s revolt but to the long persecution under Saul, inferring a protracted struggle from the “how long” of v.2. Charles Ellicott, a grammatical-historical witness, renders it “In my crying hear me,” and calls the conception of God as the eternal source of righteousness one of the noblest legacies of the Hebrew faith, summed up in the question, “Shall not the judge of all the earth do right?” John Wesley reads the title more briefly, God “the witness and defender of my righteous cause,” while the puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon marks that “God of my righteousness” is used nowhere else in Scripture, and makes God the author, witness, maintainer, judge, and rewarder of David’s righteousness, to whom he carries his suit past the petty courts of human opinion into the King’s Bench of heaven.

On the next clause the voices agree. “Thou hast enlarged me” Gill and Clarke take of a deliverance out of straits, Clarke as one brought from prison into the open; Ellicott renders it “in my straitness thou hast made room for me,” a favourite phrase of David’s recurring at Ps. 18:19; and Spurgeon pictures an army hemmed in a defile until God dashes down the rocks and gives it room. The one patristic voice, the latin-fathers Augustine of Hippo, hears the whole psalm on another register, taking its words for the words of the risen Lord, or of the believer in the Church hoping on him, and reading “in tribulation thou hast enlarged me” as the soul led out of the straits of sadness into the broad ways of joy. So the plea closes, as Henry says, on its only sure ground, “Hear me for thy mercy’s sake.”
2:
Turning from God to the men arrayed against him, David demands how long they will persist, and the witnesses first fix whom he means by “the sons of men.” The reformed John Gill takes them for the great men, the nobles of Israel drawn into the conspiracy, men of power and dignity whom the psalmist confronts. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch sharpen the Hebrew: over against “sons of Adam,” who are lost in the multitude, “sons of ish” denotes such as stand prominently out of it, so the address is aimed at the aristocratic party whose tool Absalom had become. Charles Ellicott agrees that the phrase means men of high degree — Luther’s “gentlemen” — and gathers from the reproach that the calumny uttered against the king in Jerusalem had reached his ears.

On “how long will ye turn my glory into shame” the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry hears a double charge: the sinners debase themselves, for they are “sons of men,” a word for man as a noble creature, and act beneath the dignity of their own reason; and they dishonour their Maker, turning his glory into shame as the idolaters do in Rom. 1:23 — for “glory” may be taken of God himself, whom David had just called his glory in Ps. 3:3. John Wesley refers the glory rather to the honour God had conferred on David, which his enemies laboured to turn to disgrace. Ellicott notes that the Septuagint and Vulgate followed a different and perhaps correct reading, “how long will ye be heavy of heart?”

The last charge is that they “love vanity, and seek after leasing.” Gill and Wesley gloss the pair as the wickedness and the lies — the calumnies raised to make David odious — that his enemies both loved and pursued. Clarke and Ellicott dwell on the old word: “leasing” is simply lying, a Saxon term Ellicott traces through Wycliffe’s rendering of the devil as a liar and “the father of it” in John 8:44, and on through Chaucer and Shakespeare, while Clarke reads the whole as the empty, groundless promises of Absalom’s cause. The puritan-evangelical Charles Spurgeon leads the reader from the closet of prayer into the field of conflict, admiring David’s undaunted courage: he owns his enemies to be great men, yet chides them as foolish children who make his honour a jest, and at the closing “Selah” — which Clarke marks with his own “see what the end will be” — he solemnly pauses to wonder at the grace that has taught some to love truth while others seek lies.
3:
Against their contempt David sets a fact they had overlooked, and the witnesses gather on the word “set apart.” The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reads it as a mark of ownership: the Lord has noticed the pious, benevolent, tender-hearted man and put him aside as his own property, so that to touch him is to touch what is God’s. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott traces the Hebrew verb to the severance God made between Israel and Egypt in Exod. 8:22, and takes it to mean “has distinguished or honoured”; the word rendered “godly,” he adds, is chasîd, in which the covenant relation between God and his anointed is more prominent than any moral excellence, though that is presupposed. Keil and Delitzsch, another grammatical-historical voice, read the verse as a summons to the adversaries to repent and cleave to the Lord instead of being carried away by arrogance.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the doctrine two ways. As a warning, God has set the godly apart for himself and reckons that those who touch them touch the apple of his eye, so that they offend at their peril, as the little ones of Matt. 18:6 are not to be offended and the oppressed cry is heard in Exod. 22:23; as an invitation, every particular godly man is God’s separated and sealed one, a jewel he will own in the day he makes up his treasure. Charles Spurgeon, with Henry among the puritan-evangelical voices, turns the verse to the comfort of election: the godly are the chosen of God, set apart by distinguishing grace, and though unrenewed men cannot endure the doctrine it is the guarantee of complete salvation and an argument for success at the throne of grace — he who chose us for himself will surely hear our prayers, for “shall not God avenge his own elect?”

The reformed John Gill keeps the weight on the assurance that follows, “the LORD will hear when I call unto him,” bidding the reader take notice of it and depend on it as fact. John Wesley makes the personal reference plain: the godly man is David himself, whom, though they traduce him as a hypocrite, God had pronounced a man after his own heart in 1 Sam. 13:14 and set apart to be his vicegerent on the throne. The witnesses do not divide; they agree that the election of the godly is at once the ground of David’s confidence in prayer and the peril of those who fight against a man whom God has claimed for his own.
4:
The counsel of this verse turns on a single Hebrew imperative, and here the witnesses genuinely divide over how to render it. The Authorized text has “Stand in awe, and sin not,” and the reformed John Gill takes this as the plain sense — stand in awe of God and his judgments, be afraid of him, and sin no more — yet at once records that the Septuagint, Vulgate, Syriac, Arabic, and Ethiopic all read instead “Be ye angry, and sin not,” the very words the apostle takes up in Eph. 4:26, and he weighs the two kinds of anger, the sinful that is without cause or beyond measure, and the righteous that is kindled not against persons but against sin. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch go further and judge that the Septuagint “has rendered it correctly,” hearing a warning against blind passion: if ye will be angry, beware of sinning. Adam Clarke, among the wesleyan-arminian voices, leans the same way, paraphrasing, “if ye be angry, and if ye think ye have cause to be angry, do not let your disaffection carry you to acts of rebellion against both God and your king.”

The other grammatical-historical witness resists that reading outright. Charles Ellicott grants that “be angry” is etymologically correct and rightly quoted at Ephesians, but calls it “plainly inadmissible here,” rendering the word “tremble,” whether with fear or with awe. John Wesley keeps the same reverential sense — “be afraid, if not of me, yet of God, who hath engaged in my cause” — and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, though he notes the Septuagint’s “be angry” in passing, expounds the clause as a call to a holy reverence of the majesty of God and a holy dread of his wrath. Charles Spurgeon presses it as experience: “tremble and sin not — how many reverse this counsel and sin but tremble not,” and bids the rash sinner go to his bed and think upon his ways. So the division is real, between those who hear a caution against sinful anger and those who hear a summons to reverent fear.

On the rest of the verse the witnesses close ranks. “Commune with your own heart upon your bed” they take as a call to solitary self-examination in the quiet of the night, Henry pointing to David’s own practice of remembering God upon his bed in Ps. 63:6 and bidding the sinner ask conscience a question before turning to sleep; and “be still,” which Clarke renders “be dumb,” they read as the composing of a tumultuous mind, that the soul may hear what God and conscience have to say.
5:
From awe and self-communing David moves the rebels to worship, and the witnesses read “the sacrifices of righteousness” along converging lines. The reformed John Gill gathers several senses: sacrifices of things righteously gotten, since God hates robbery for burnt offering; sacrifices offered according to the law, without blemish; above all sacrifices offered in the faith of the great sacrifice to come, without which faith it is impossible to please God — and he notes that righteousness may also bear the sense of alms and beneficence, acts of mercy God prefers to ceremonial offerings, adding that the sacrifices of a broken and a contrite heart are of all the most esteemed by God. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott takes the phrase more narrowly as “right” or “due” sacrifices, offerings duly and religiously performed, comparing the like expression in Deut. 33:19. Keil and Delitzsch join the offering to the trust that follows, reading the verse as the counsel that turns the disaffected from their discontent back to the Lord.

The wesleyan-arminian voices press the heart behind the offering. Adam Clarke warns that no sacrifice offered in the midst of rebellious conduct can be received — such a sacrifice would itself be a sin — and lifts the lesson to the gospel, that under the new covenant no offering is accepted but through the one all-atoning sacrifice of Christ, by whom alone a sinner’s mouth is opened to plead with God. John Wesley likewise requires that the persons offering be righteous and offer with an honest mind, with faith and true repentance, without which all their sacrifices are of no esteem with God.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the two halves together: we must not only cease to do evil but learn to do well, for the sacrifices of righteousness are good works, the fruits of the reigning love of God and neighbour, better than all burnt-offerings, while the offering of the unrighteous God counts an abomination, as in Isa. 1:11; and having offered them, we are welcome to the second charge, “put your trust in the LORD” — to serve God without diffidence or any fear of losing by him, honouring him by trusting in him only and not in wealth or an arm of flesh, and leaning not to our own understanding. Charles Spurgeon hears the whole gospel in the exhortation: when the Jew offered sacrifice righteously, in a spiritual manner, he set forth the Redeemer, the great sin-atoning Lamb, so that the verse points sinners to place their whole confidence in him who died for men and is the Lord Jehovah. The witnesses agree that right worship and settled trust are the way back for men estranged from God.
6:
“There be many that say, Who will shew us any good?” — and the witnesses divide over whose despairing question this is. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott hears it from within David’s own camp: around the fugitive king were many whose courage was not so high nor their faith so firm as his, and he catches their expressions of despair, keeping the Authorized Version’s future, “who will shew us,” rather than turning it into a wish. Keil and Delitzsch read it likewise, as the voice of companions whose long tribulation has turned their hope to despair, so that the king must pray the light of God’s countenance upon them all. John Wesley too takes the “many” for David’s own followers, grown weary of waiting upon God and longing for someone to end their troubles. The reformed John Gill allows this among his options — the men with David wishing themselves home, or the enemies wishing Absalom’s cause might prosper — but sets first the reading that the many are carnal, worldly-minded men seeking after temporal good and resting in it.

That worldly reading the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes his own and turns into a searching contrast: the foolish wish asks in general “Who will make us happy?” without applying to God who alone can; it seeks a good that may be seen, and no good that is out of sight and the object of faith only, looking no further than the eye of sense where the believer looks with an eye of faith, as in 2 Cor. 4:18; and it asks for any good, not the chief good — good meat, good drink, a good trade, a good estate — when any good will serve the turn of most men, but a gracious soul will not be put off so. Charles Spurgeon owns that the craving to see rather than believe is “the tendency of us all,” found even among David’s own followers, while for the worldling it is an unceasing cry; the believer’s face, he says, is turned upward like the angels’, and the light of God’s countenance is enough for him. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke objects that the word “any” is not in the text at all — the cry is simply “Who will shew us good?”, the universal search of man for a good to content his heart, which most men mistake for the gratification of the senses.

Over against that wish the godly make their choice, and here the witnesses are one, praying with David, “LORD, lift thou up the light of thy countenance upon us.” Clarke names this the one thing needful, the peace and approbation of God that the worldling misses; and Ellicott hears in it an echo of the priestly benediction of Num. 6:24, reading the anomalous Hebrew for “lift up” as a play on the word for a banner, a sign to the fearful that the Lord’s power was ready to protect their king. So the many crave a good they can see, and the few crave the face of God.
7:
The psalm now turns from petition to the joy that answers it, and with the worldlings’ wish for corn and wine still in view the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry weighs the gladness David has found instead. The good those worldlings had wished for, Henry observes, was just this increase of their corn and their wine, the plenty of the field; and it is in the very season of such increase that David owns a gladness God has given him which far outgoes it. This, he says, is what the godly rejoice in above anything: God had put gladness into David’s heart, not merely supporting and refreshing him but filling him with a joy unspeakable, and therefore it is what he will still pursue and seek after all the days of his life. When God puts grace in the heart, Henry observes, he puts gladness in the heart; nor is any joy comparable to that which gracious souls have in the communications of the divine favour — not even the joy of harvest, of a plentiful harvest, when the corn and the wine increase.

Henry marks the contrast the verse itself draws. The mirth of worldly people is but a flash, a shadow; even in their laughter the heart is sorrowful, as the proverb has it in Prov. 14:13, and the end of that mirth is heaviness. But the gladness God gives is inward, solid, substantial joy, seated in the heart and not on the surface; “thou hast given gladness in my heart,” Henry notes, is the very turn of the words. True joy, he insists, is God’s gift, and not as the world giveth, according to the promise of John 14:27 — the world can neither give this joy nor take it away.

From this Henry draws the pastoral lesson the verse presses. The saints have no reason to envy carnal worldlings their mirth and their increase; they should rather pity them, for the men who seek their portion in corn and wine might know a better gladness and will not. Many inquire after happiness, asking with the many of the verse before, “Who will shew us any good?”, but David had found it, and found it not in the abundance of the field but in the countenance of God. So the single witness leaves the verse as a quiet triumph of faith over sense: a heart made glad by God outweighs the fullest barn, and the joy that comes down from the light of God’s face is worth more than the richest harvest the worldling can desire.
8:
“I will both lay me down in peace, and sleep” — the psalm ends in the calm of a man who can rest because God keeps him, and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry unfolds the whole of that confidence. David had laid himself down and slept before, as the morning hymn recalls in Ps. 3:5, and so he will still: having the assurance of God’s favour, he will lie down in peace, and with as much pleasure as those whose corn and wine increase, who lie down as Boaz did in his threshing-floor when his heart was merry in Ruth 3:7 — for, as the verse says, the LORD only makes him to dwell in safety. Though he is alone, Henry adds, yet he is not alone, for God is with him; though he has no guards to attend him, the Lord alone is sufficient to protect him.

Henry gathers the safety of the verse into three assurances. First, David can enjoy himself: his soul returns to God and reposes in him as its rest, and so he lays himself down and sleeps in peace, sure that nothing can come amiss to him. Second, he fears no disturbance from his enemies but sleeps quietly and secure, because God himself has undertaken to keep him safe; and when he comes at last to sleep the sleep of death and to make his bed in the darkness of the grave, he will then, with good old Simeon, depart in peace, as in Luke 2:29, assured that God will receive his soul and that his body too shall dwell in safety in the grave. Third, he commits all his affairs to God and contentedly leaves the issue with him.

That last point Henry likens to the husbandman who, having cast his seed into the ground, sleeps and rises night and day while the seed springs and grows he knows not how, in the manner of Mark 4:26. So a good man, having by faith and prayer cast his care upon God, sleeps and rests night and day and is very easy, leaving it to his God to perform all things for him and prepared to welcome his holy will. The single witness closes the psalm where it began, in the mercy of God: the same favour that enlarged David in his distress now lays him down in peace, so that the evening prayer ends not in fear but in sleep, and the last word of the psalm is safety.
